programme: Wong ancestry-recombination graphs · deterministic canonical normal form
title: A finite ancestry graph has a precise sample-preserving simplification

plain_language.question: Can local common-ancestor truncation, unary bypass and interval merging be joined in one exact finite-graph theorem?
plain_language.what_we_learned: Yes. The result constructs a finite graph with the stated local edges, protected samples, relevant preserved paths and canonical interval storage. The assumptions distinguish sampled ancestors, unsupported edges and isolated original IDs.
plain_language.what_it_lets_someone_do: Use a precise mathematical target for a later simplifier/exporter, including what it must preserve and what it deliberately removes.
plain_language.what_cannot_conclude: The whole-graph adapter is noncomputable. Only the interval-list merger is executable; storage idempotence is not full-pipeline idempotence, and no stochastic law, timestamps, production software or empirical accuracy is certified.

exact_statement_and_scope: For every finite GARG with globally acyclic union topology, a fixed finite node catalogue and sample set, and each record annotated by a finite family of proper pairwise-disjoint half-open intervals in an arbitrary linear order, first retain precisely the active edges whose child is sample-ancestral but is not a reflexive common ancestor of all designated samples at that coordinate. Then contract paths through nodes that are neither samples nor locally branching vertices of that truncated sample ancestry. The retained set may depend on coordinate; its constancy on automatically derived source breakpoint cells is proved for this rule. The composed theorem constructs an actual finite H on the same node type and sample set. Its local edges are exactly that contraction. H is sample-supported, introduces no new breakpoints and has one nonempty record per active ordered parent-child pair, with strictly separated maximal intervals. Sample-to-sample ancestry paths are exactly preserved. For nonempty samples and a supplied IsMRCA witness, paths from that MRCA to each sample are exactly preserved. At each coordinate where the original graph has unique parents, H also has unique parents and every incident nonsample node has at least two distinct children. Protected sampled ancestors may remain unary, and unused original IDs may remain isolated. An MRCA means a common ancestor below every common ancestor. Unique existence is proved under nonempty samples, unique local parents and existence of some common ancestor; it is not presumed for arbitrary DAGs. The truncation construction is total without an MRCA-existence assumption. Empty and singleton sample sets give no retained edges; without a common ancestor it reduces to ordinary sample-support filtering. This operation deliberately removes supported material above a local MRCA and is not identical to support restriction. Independently, canonical interval storage preserves the full indexed local-edge relation and sample set. Equal full local-edge semantics and samples yield exactly equal canonical graphs; empty-annotation ghost records can disappear. Canonicalizing H again gives H. This is storage idempotence, not a claim of full truncation/contraction-pipeline idempotence. The executable touching-interval list merge preserves union membership for every list and, on sorted nonoverlapping inputs, produces the unique strictly separated interval list, is idempotent and reuses input endpoints. The whole-graph canonicalization and composed normal form use classical finite enumeration/activity decisions. No computable whole-exporter or runtime conclusion follows. No probability law, physical dates, event history or empirical ancestry inference is claimed preserved.
